overview.text: The Randolph Urban Renewal Project (Project Va. R-58) is a federally assisted urban renewal program in a 380-acre, roughly 98% Black neighborhood in Richmond, Virginia, where the Richmond Redevelopment and Housing Authority proposes to demolish about 1,117 residential buildings, rehabilitate about 1,053 others, relocate approximately 1,814 families and individuals plus 49 businesses, and rebuild housing and infrastructure over an estimated eight years at a gross cost of about $34.7 million. The neighborhood is a lower-income community of about 9,000 residents (mean 1969 family income $7,226 versus $10,620 citywide, 22% at or below poverty) that includes 748 people 65 or older on Social Security and four elementary schools serving 1,567 children. HUD considered three alternatives — no action, a smaller project limited to redevelopment (dropping rehabilitation), or moving the project elsewhere — and rejected all three in favor of the proposed action. The largest adverse environmental impact identified is the adjacent, non-federally funded Downtown Expressway, whose projected 1985 traffic of 56,000 vehicles per day would add thousands of kilograms per day of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, and nitrogen oxides to the northern edge of the neighborhood, an impact the EIS calls 'almost impossible to correct or even mitigate,' to be partly buffered by a 15-foot landscaped earth berm along Grayland Avenue; long-term effects on the neighborhood itself are described as beneficial. The plan was developed over about 24 months with the elected 30-member Randolph Planning Study Board and, after early opposition in 1969, was ultimately supported at public hearings and endorsed by the City Planning Commission, the Regional Planning Commission, and most reviewing agencies, though EPA gave a 'LO-2' rating requesting a proper carbon-monoxide dispersion analysis and one Planning Commission member abstained over expressway concerns.

project_description.text: The Randolph Urban Renewal Project (Project Va. R-58) is a federally assisted (HUD Title I) redevelopment and rehabilitation program covering a 380-acre neighborhood in Richmond, Virginia, bounded roughly by Byrd Park, Cary Street, Colorado Avenue, and Riverview Cemetery. Over an estimated seven-to-eight years, the Richmond Redevelopment and Housing Authority would demolish 1,117 residential structures (1,613 dwelling units) and 58 non-residential buildings, rehabilitate 1,053 residential and 52 non-residential buildings, and relocate about 1,814 families and individuals plus roughly 49 businesses and 13 non-profits, aiming to keep about the same residential density but upgrade housing quality. Physical work includes extending and widening streets such as Harrison Street and Grayland Avenue, separating the existing combined sewer into sanitary and storm systems, and placing electric and telephone lines underground within the redevelopment area, with total gross project cost estimated at about $34.7 million and a federal capital grant of about $22.8 million. The renewal area is bordered on the north by the separately built, toll-financed Downtown Expressway, a six-lane controlled-access highway whose noise and air-quality effects the plan is designed to buffer.

affected_community.text: Randolph is a predominantly Black lower-income neighborhood in Richmond's West End, home to about 9,000 people, 98% of whom are Black, with 1,086 homeowners, 1,679 renters, and 183 roomers or boarders; at the time of a full survey only three white families lived in the area. Mean 1969 family income was $7,226 versus $10,620 citywide (and only $5,939 in census tract 413), 22% of Randolph families were at or below poverty (27.8% in tract 413), 12% received public assistance, and 748 people 65 or older received Social Security. Despite 63% of residents being renters, 58% had lived at the same address for the previous five years. Those to be relocated include 141 elderly families, 981 elderly individuals, and 37 families of 8 or more people; the neighborhood also contains four elementary schools (Randolph, Clark-Springs, Amelia-Maymont, and West End) serving 1,567 K–5 children, churches, and the Virginia Home for the Incurables. Adjacent communities are the largely white, low-income Oregon Hill to the east and the Black, single-family Maymont community (about 2,000 residents) to the south and west.

alternatives_overview.text: HUD considered three alternatives to the proposed action: (1) 'no action' — leave Randolph as is, which HUD says would waste the two years of citizen planning and allow continued deterioration while the Downtown Expressway is built anyway; (2) reduce the project's size by dropping the rehabilitation portion and treating only the redevelopment area (about two-thirds smaller), which HUD rejects because 'borderline' areas would become new sources of blight; and (3) relocate the project to another Richmond neighborhood, which HUD says would let Randolph's blight spread across all 380 acres and 12,000 residents. HUD concludes 'the balance appears obviously to be in favor of the proposed action.' Within the chosen plan, alternative design choices considered include a mix of rehabilitation in 'conservation areas' with redevelopment in blighted areas, a variety of housing types (townhouses, garden apartments, single-family homes) for low- and moderate-income families, scattered-site public housing rather than one or two large complexes, and an alternative street alignment extending a new street through vacant cemetery land to divert non-community traffic around Randolph.

environmental_impact.text: Short-term adverse impacts during multi-year construction include dust, noise, erosion, traffic disruption, partially demolished structures, temporary loss of street trees and recreation areas, and the temporary (and in a few cases permanent) relocation of residents. The largest ongoing adverse impact is attributed to the adjacent Downtown Expressway (not federally funded), whose projected 1985 traffic of about 56,000 vehicles per day would add roughly 5,176.6 kg/day of carbon monoxide, 766.6 kg/day of hydrocarbons, and 858.5 kg/day of nitrogen oxides — an impact described as 'almost impossible to correct or even mitigate' — on top of existing air that already exceeds the National Ambient Air Quality Standard for suspended particulates (88 µg/m³ quarterly mean versus a 75 µg/m³ annual standard). To meet HUD interior-noise criteria (no more than 45 dBA in sleeping quarters for 8 hours in 24) and exterior levels, consultants Bolt, Beranek and Newman recommend a 15-foot landscaped earth berm along Grayland Avenue (a 10-foot barrier was much less effective, a 20-foot only marginally better) plus building orientation, air conditioning, fixed glazing, and solid-core doors; predicted noise curves at sampled locations remained in the 'Normally Acceptable' range and did not cross the 'Unacceptable' line (75 dBA for more than 8 hours). The State Water Control Board concluded the project would not create additional water pollution problems if separate sanitary and storm sewers are installed to the fullest extent feasible. The Virginia Historic Landmarks Commission found most demolition-zone structures to have 'little redeeming architectural value' but flagged the 200–400 blocks of Randolph Street, the 400–500 blocks of Harrison, the Italianate Randolph School, and the frame Queen Anne RCAP Center as possibly worth conservation. Long-term effects on the neighborhood itself are described as beneficial: replacement of blight and substandard housing, improved utilities, and reduced noise/visual impact from the expressway.

public_response.text: Citizen involvement was extensive and organized through the elected 30-member Randolph Planning Study Board (RPSB), which grew out of earlier neighborhood groups formed in 1969 and worked with the Richmond Redevelopment and Housing Authority for 24 months to develop the plan. Early resident reaction was hostile — at a February 23, 1969 meeting at Sixth Baptist Church 'there was strong community opposition' — but by a November 19, 1972 public meeting the community voted to accept the plan, and a later Amelia School hearing drew more than 300 people, most in favor; residents' main questions concerned relocation payments. The Regional Planning Commission unanimously approved the plan on January 27, 1972, and the City Planning Commission recommended approval on December 5, 1972, with member Mrs. Douglas C. Burke abstaining over concerns about the Downtown Expressway. Of 14 federal, state, and local agencies asked to comment on the draft EIS, nine responded; the Richmond City Council, City Manager, Virginia Department of Health, Virginia Department of Highways, FAA, and HEW supported or did not object, while EPA gave a 'LO-2' rating — no objection but requesting a proper carbon-monoxide dispersion analysis for the Downtown Expressway — and the Federal Highway Administration objected that the EIS improperly attributed adverse impacts of the non-federal expressway to the Randolph project, an objection HUD rejected.

summary_of_interest.claim: A federal urban renewal EIS proposes to demolish 1,117 buildings and relocate about 1,814 families plus 49 businesses in a neighborhood that is 98% Black — with only three white families identified in a full survey — making this a large-magnitude displacement concentrated almost entirely on Black residents.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: The majority off the persons to be displaced by the Randolph Urban Renewal Program are black. At the time of the 100 percent survey three white families resided within the area.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: The document records that a federally funded clearance program of this scale falls almost exclusively on a single racial community, a demographic concentration the EIS itself documents on this page.

evidence.quote: The majority off the persons to be displaced by the Randolph Urban Renewal Program are black. At the time of the 100 percent survey three white families resided within the area.

summary_of_interest.claim: HUD and the Federal Highway Administration openly disagree over whether the EIS should even analyze the adjacent Downtown Expressway; FHWA argued its impacts are 'alleged effects that will be caused by some other action,' while HUD invoked NEPA §102(2)C to insist on including them.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: This summary should be limited to the probable adverse environmental effects as a result of the proposed action (i.e. Randolph Plan) not alleged effects that will be caused by some other action (i.e. Downtown Expressway).
summary_of_interest.why_notable: This is a substantive inter-agency dispute over NEPA scope — whether a federal EIS must analyze a non-federal, locally financed project running through the same neighborhood.
